proof.text: Write $G=\operatorname{Aut}_K(L)$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-finite-galois-fixed-field] to the finite normal separable extension $L/K$: $G$ is finite and $|G|=[L:K]$. In particular its subgroups $D$ and $I$ are finite. Apply [lem-exc-dvr-galois-degree-data] to $A,L,B$. Let $X$ be its finite set of maximal ideals, $g=|X|>0$, and $f=[B/\mathfrak n:k]>0$. Its common ramification index at $\mathfrak n$ is precisely the $e$ in the item: both are the exponent of $t$ in $\pi_A=u t^e$. Therefore $|G|=g e f$, and $G$ acts transitively on $X$.

source.place: Tag 09EE (lemma-galois-inertia), first proof paragraph, recalling Tags 09E8, 09EA and 09EB.

proof.text: The map $G\to X$, $\sigma\mapsto\sigma(\mathfrak n)$, is onto by Step 1. Two elements $\sigma,\tau$ have the same image exactly when $\tau^{-1}\sigma\in D$, so each fibre is a coset $\tau D$, in bijection with $D$ by left multiplication. Counting these disjoint fibres gives $|G|=g|D|$. Comparing with $g e f$ and cancelling the positive integer $g$ gives $|D|=ef$.

source.place: Tag 09EE (lemma-galois-inertia), first paragraph, stabilizer order calculation; coset counting written out.

proof.text: Put $E=B/\mathfrak n$. By [lem-exc-dvr-residue-normal-action], $E/k$ is normal and the residue-action homomorphism $\rho:D\to\operatorname{Aut}_k(E)$ is surjective. Its kernel consists exactly of the elements acting trivially on $E$, namely the subgroup $I$ defined in the item. The extension $E/k$ is finite of degree $f$ by Step 1. Its characteristic is $p$, since its field embedding from $k$ is injective: a multiple of $1$ vanishes in $E$ exactly when the same multiple vanishes in $k$.

source.place: Tag 09EE (lemma-galois-inertia), first paragraph, applying Tag 09ED (lemma-galois-galois) without a separable-residue assumption.

proof.text: The automorphism group of $E/k$ is finite, as it is the surjective image of the finite group $D$ from Step 3; denote its order by $h\geq1$. Apply [lem-exc-normal-field-degree-factors] to the finite normal extension $E/k$ in characteristic $p$. With its notation, $h=s$, $f=s d$ and $d=p^c$ for some $c\geq0$. Substitution gives $f=h p^c$. This is exactly where a possible inseparable residue degree is retained.

source.place: Tag 09EE (lemma-galois-inertia), first paragraph, invoking fields.tex Tag 09HS and the discussion after Tag 030L.

proof.text: Every fibre of the onto homomorphism $\rho$ in Step 3 is a coset of $I$: if $\rho(\sigma)=\rho(\tau)$ then $\tau^{-1}\sigma\in I$, and the converse follows by applying $\rho$. Left multiplication identifies each fibre with $I$, so $|D|=|I|h$. Using Steps 2 and 4 gives $|I|h=ef=e h p^c$. Cancel the positive integer $h$ to obtain $|I|=e p^c$. The characteristic satisfies $p>1$, since $1\ne0$ in $k$, and it is prime: if $p=ab$ with $1<a,b<p$, then $(a\cdot1)(b\cdot1)=0$ in $k$ although neither factor vanishes, contrary to $k$ being a field. To express the result using $n$, write the prime factorization of the positive integer $e$ as $e=p^a m$ with $a\geq0$ and $p\nmid m$. Every divisor of $e$ prime to $p$ divides $m$, and $m$ is itself such a divisor; hence the largest such divisor is $n=m$. Thus $|I|=n p^{a+c}$, proving the claim with $b=a+c\geq0$.

title: Prime-to-residue-characteristic part of finite inertia order
statement: Let $A$ be a discrete valuation ring [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring], with fraction field $K$ and residue field $k$ of characteristic $p>0$. Let $L/K$ be a finite normal separable field extension [def-pc-field-extension, def-weil-pbc-separable-algebraic-extension], let $B$ be the integral closure of $A$ in $L$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure], and let $\mathfrak n$ be a maximal ideal of $B$. Suppose $C=B_{\mathfrak n}$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime] is a discrete valuation ring and the structural map $A\to C$ is local. For uniformizers $\pi_A$ of $A$ and $t$ of $C$, define the positive integer $e$ by $\pi_A=ut^e$ with $u\in C^\times$. Define $D=\{\sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}(L/K):\sigma(\mathfrak n)=\mathfrak n\}$ and $I=\{\sigma\in D:\sigma|_{B/\mathfrak n}=1\}$. Then $I$ is finite. If $n$ is the largest divisor of $e$ prime to $p$, then $|I|=n p^b$ for some integer $b\geq0$. No separability of $(B/\mathfrak n)/k$ is assumed.
